Non-Surgical Breast Enlargement

PRP and Breast Enhancement: Evidence Explained

Platelet-rich plasma is prepared from your own blood to concentrate platelets. Its effects depend entirely on the specific indication and the evidence available for it.

Home/Non-Surgical Breast Enlargement/PRP and Breast Enhancement: Evidence Explained

How PRP is prepared

PRP is prepared by taking a sample of the patient’s own blood and processing it to concentrate the platelets. The resulting preparation is intended for specific purposes; those purposes are not interchangeable, and a preparation intended for one indication is not automatically appropriate for another.

PRP and breast enhancement

Claims about PRP and breast enhancement should be assessed against appropriate clinical evidence for the precise procedure being offered. The evidence for a particular use should be established before that use is described as effective.

What this page should explain

Key points

How PRP is prepared

What it is intended to do, and why preparation and indication matter.

Procedure-related risks

Possible pain, bruising, bleeding, infection and other procedure-related risks.

Clinician review

Why suitability and expected outcomes require review by a qualified clinician, with reference to local regulatory requirements.

Research vs. established use

There is an important difference between studying a treatment and establishing that it is safe and effective for a particular purpose. Claims of breast enhancement should be assessed against appropriate clinical evidence for the precise procedure offered.

What to ask

Ask what evidence supports the specific use, what the known risks are, and what regulatory requirements apply to that intended use in your jurisdiction.

Further reading from the consolidated article

  • U.S. FDA — Dermal fillers and their approved uses
  • U.S. FDA — Regenerative medicine and stem cell safety

Questions

PRP FAQs

PRP should not be marketed as a proven method of increasing breast size without robust evidence supporting that particular use. Effects depend on the specific indication and the available evidence.

Using your own blood reduces some risks but does not remove them. Any procedure carries procedure-related risks such as pain, bruising, bleeding or infection, and suitability still requires clinical review.
